expectedText:
HEAT ILLNESS PREVENTION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Acme Corp

ABOUT THIS HEAT ILLNESS PREVENTION INFORMATION SHEET
This Heat Illness Prevention — Information Sheet describes California's Cal/OSHA heat illness prevention standards for outdoor places of employment, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3395, and for indoor places of employment, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3396, as those requirements relate to the working relationship between Jordan Alex Lee and Acme Corp.

It summarizes selected requirements of those two regulations: which outdoor and indoor workplaces they cover and at what temperatures, the requirement to provide access to drinking water, the requirement to provide access to shade (outdoors) or a cool-down area (indoors), the additional procedures required at higher temperature thresholds, the requirement to closely observe newly assigned and heat-wave-exposed employees during an acclimatization period, the training that must be given to employees and supervisors, and the requirement to maintain a written Heat Illness Prevention Plan.

This topic is distinct from this corpus's Injury and Illness Prevention Program (IIPP) — Information Sheet, which describes California's general written workplace-safety-program requirement under Labor Code § 6401.7 and 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203, and from this corpus's Workplace Violence Prevention Plan — Information Sheet, which describes a different specific workplace hazard under Labor Code § 6401.9. Both the outdoor and indoor heat illness standards state that their required measures may instead be integrated into an employer's IIPP.

Acme Corp has identified Taylor Morgan as the person responsible for heat illness prevention matters described in this information sheet.

This information sheet is not itself Acme Corp's written Heat Illness Prevention Plan, does not itself satisfy 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3395's or § 3396's written-plan requirement, and does not determine that any particular practice of Acme Corp's is or is not compliant with California law.

WHICH OUTDOOR AND INDOOR WORKPLACES ARE COVERED
California has two separate Cal/OSHA heat illness prevention regulations, one for outdoor places of employment and one for indoor places of employment. The outdoor standard, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3395(a)(1), states that it 'shall apply to all outdoor places of employment.' Within that broad outdoor coverage, § 3395(a)(2) lists a narrower set of industries that must also comply with the standard's high-heat procedures (addressed in a companion clause of this information sheet): agriculture, construction, landscaping, oil and gas extraction, and the transportation or delivery of agricultural products, construction materials, or other heavy materials. An employer in an industry not on that list is not required to comply with the high-heat-procedures subsection, per the exception stated directly under § 3395(a)(1).

The indoor standard, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3396(a)(1), applies on its own terms to 'all indoor work areas where the temperature equals or exceeds 82 degrees Fahrenheit when employees are present.' A narrower set of conditions then triggers full coverage under the indoor standard, including its assessment-and-control-measures subsection: § 3396(a)(2)(A) provides that full coverage applies where 'the temperature equals or exceeds 87 degrees Fahrenheit when employees are present,' and the same subsection separately triggers full coverage where the heat index reaches 87 degrees Fahrenheit, where employees wear clothing that restricts heat removal and the temperature reaches 82 degrees Fahrenheit, or where employees work in a high radiant heat area at 82 degrees Fahrenheit. The indoor standard also states exceptions for teleworking from a location not under the employer's control, for certain brief incidental heat exposures, for emergency operations, and for specified state and local confinement facilities.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]

  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3395 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 3395, subd. (a)(1) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/3395.html)
  "If an industry is not listed in subsection (a)(2), employers in that industry are not required to comply with subsection (e), High-heat procedures."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3395 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 3395, subd. (a) exception (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/3395.html)
  "This section applies to all indoor work areas where the temperature equals or exceeds 82 degrees Fahrenheit when employees are present."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3396 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 3396, subd. (a)(1) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/3396.html)
  "The temperature equals or exceeds 87 degrees Fahrenheit when employees are present; or"
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3396 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 3396, subd. (a)(2)(A) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/3396.html)
  Known gap: This clause draws on two formally independent Cal/OSHA regulations — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3395 (outdoor) and § 3396 (indoor) — codified and adopted separately, not two subdivisions of one section; each section's own quotations in this clause, however, are drawn from subdivisions of that same section (§ 3395(a)(1) and (a)(2) are both part of § 3395; § 3396(a)(1) and (a)(2)(A) are both part of § 3396), so within each regulation the citations are not independent corroborating sources of each other. This document did not independently quote the indoor standard's teleworking, incidental-exposure, emergency-operations, or confinement-facility exceptions, or its 'Order to Take Special Action' provision in § 3396(a)(3); they are described here only in summary based on the fetched text, and their precise conditions and exact wording are not reproduced as citations. This is a description of what these regulations require in general, not a determination of whether any specific workplace of the employer's is or is not covered.

ACCESS TO DRINKING WATER
Both the outdoor and indoor standards impose the same core drinking-water access requirement in nearly identical language. The outdoor standard, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3395(c), requires that 'Employees shall have access to potable drinking water meeting the requirements of Sections 1524, 3363, and 3457, as applicable, including but not limited to the requirements that it be fresh, pure, suitably cool, and provided to employees free of charge.' The indoor standard, § 3396(c), states the same requirement using the same cross-referenced sections. Both standards further require that where drinking water is not plumbed or otherwise continuously supplied, it 'shall be provided in sufficient quantity at the beginning of the work shift to provide one quart per employee per hour for drinking for the entire shift,' quoting § 3395(c); § 3396(c) states the identical one-quart-per-employee-per-hour quantity requirement, and both allow an employer to begin a shift with a smaller quantity if it has effective procedures to replenish water during the shift as needed.

  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3395 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 3395, subd. (c) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/3395.html)
  "Where drinking water is not plumbed or otherwise continuously supplied, it shall be provided in sufficient quantity at the beginning of the work shift to provide one quart per employee per hour for drinking for the entire shift."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3395 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 3395, subd. (c) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/3395.html)
  "Employees shall have access to potable drinking water meeting the requirements of sections 1524, 3363, and 3457, as applicable, including but not limited to the requirements that it be fresh, pure, suitably cool, and provided to employees free of charge."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3396 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 3396, subd. (c) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/3396.html)
  Known gap: This clause quotes both § 3395(c) and § 3396(c) because they are formally independent regulations, each separately adopted, even though their water-access language is nearly identical to one another; within each regulation, the quotations are drawn from a single subdivision, (c), not from separate independent parts of that regulation. This clause does not quote or independently verify the specific technical water-quality requirements of the cross-referenced sections — 8 Cal. Code Regs. §§ 1524, 3363, and 3457 — which were not separately fetched for this document; it states only that the heat illness standards themselves cross-reference those sections. This is a description of a general regulatory requirement, not a determination of whether water has actually been made available at any particular worksite.

ACCESS TO SHADE (OUTDOORS) AND COOL-DOWN AREAS (INDOORS)
The outdoor standard ties the shade requirement to a specific temperature threshold. 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3395(d)(1) states: 'Shade shall be present when the temperature exceeds 80 degrees Fahrenheit.' Once that threshold is crossed, the employer must maintain one or more shaded areas at all times employees are present, and the amount of shade present 'shall be at least enough to accommodate the number of employees on recovery or rest periods, so that they can sit in a normal posture fully in the shade without having to be in physical contact with each other,' per the same subdivision. Below 80 degrees Fahrenheit, § 3395(d)(2) requires the employer either to provide shade on the same terms or to provide timely access to shade upon an employee's request. Employees must be allowed and encouraged to take a preventative cool-down rest in the shade whenever they feel the need to do so, per § 3395(d)(3).

The indoor standard uses the term 'cool-down area' rather than shade, and adds a temperature ceiling for that area. 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3396(d)(1) requires the employer to have and maintain one or more cool-down areas at all times employees are present, sized on the same normal-posture, no-physical-contact standard as the outdoor shade requirement, and states that 'the temperature in indoor cool-down areas shall be maintained at less than 82 degrees Fahrenheit, unless the employer demonstrates it is infeasible.'

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "Shade shall be present when the temperature exceeds 80 degrees Fahrenheit."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3395 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 3395, subd. (d)(1) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/3395.html)
  "The amount of shade present shall be at least enough to accommodate the number of employees on recovery or rest periods, so that they can sit in a normal posture fully in the shade without having to be in physical contact with each other."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3395 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 3395, subd. (d)(1) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/3395.html)
  "The temperature in indoor cool-down areas shall be maintained at less than 82 degrees Fahrenheit, unless the employer demonstrates it is infeasible."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3396 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 3396, subd. (d)(1) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/3396.html)
  Known gap: This clause quotes both § 3395(d) and § 3396(d) because they are formally independent regulations; within § 3395, the two quoted passages are both drawn from subdivision (d)(1), not from independent parts of that regulation. The outdoor standard's shade-adequacy definition (what counts as sufficient blockage of sunlight, found in § 3395(b)'s definition of 'Shade') and the indoor standard's parallel 'cool-down area' definition in § 3396(b)(4) were reviewed in the course of this research but are not separately quoted or summarized in this clause; readers should not assume this clause states every detail of either definition. This is a description of a general regulatory requirement, not a determination of whether shade or a cool-down area has actually been provided at any particular worksite.

ADDITIONAL REQUIREMENTS AT HIGHER TEMPERATURES
Both standards impose additional obligations once the temperature crosses a second, higher threshold, beyond the water and shade/cool-down requirements described elsewhere in this information sheet. Under the outdoor standard, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3395(e) provides: 'The employer shall implement high-heat procedures when the temperature equals or exceeds 95 degrees Fahrenheit,' and those procedures — required only of the specific industries listed in § 3395(a)(2) — include maintaining effective communication with employees, observing employees for signs of heat illness, designating employees authorized to call for emergency medical services, reminding employees to drink water, and holding pre-shift meetings. For employees in agriculture specifically, § 3395(e)(6) requires that 'the employer shall ensure that the employee takes a minimum ten minute net preventative cool-down rest period every two hours' once temperatures reach 95 degrees or above.

The indoor standard instead requires the employer to measure temperature and heat index and apply control measures once a work area meets one of the § 3396(a)(2) conditions described in a companion clause of this information sheet. 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3396(e)(2)(A) requires that 'Engineering controls shall be used to reduce and maintain both the temperature and heat index to below 87 degrees Fahrenheit when employees are present, or to reduce the temperature to below 82 degrees Fahrenheit where employees wear clothing that restricts heat removal or work in high radiant heat areas, except to the extent that the employer demonstrates such controls are infeasible.' Where feasible engineering controls are not sufficient to reach those thresholds, the same subdivision requires the use of administrative controls and, where still insufficient, personal heat-protective equipment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "The employer shall implement high-heat procedures when the temperature equals or exceeds 95 degrees Fahrenheit."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3395 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 3395, subd. (e) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/3395.html)
  "the employer shall ensure that the employee takes a minimum ten minute net preventative cool-down rest period every two hours."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3395 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 3395, subd. (e)(6) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/3395.html)
  "Engineering controls shall be used to reduce and maintain both the temperature and heat index to below 87 degrees Fahrenheit when employees are present, or to reduce the temperature to below 82 degrees Fahrenheit where employees wear clothing that restricts heat removal or work in high radiant heat areas, except to the extent that the employer demonstrates such controls are infeasible."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3396 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 3396, subd. (e)(2)(A) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/3396.html)
  Known gap: This clause describes two distinct regulatory mechanisms that both key off elevated temperature but are not the same requirement: the outdoor standard's 'high-heat procedures' at 95 degrees Fahrenheit (a fixed, industry-limited list of procedural obligations), and the indoor standard's tiered engineering-control, administrative-control, and personal-protective-equipment hierarchy aimed at keeping the workplace below 87 (or 82) degrees Fahrenheit. This clause does not independently quote or summarize every high-heat procedure listed in § 3395(e)(1) through (e)(5), or the indoor standard's administrative-control and personal-heat-protective-equipment provisions in § 3396(e)(2)(B) and (e)(2)(C) beyond noting that they apply when engineering controls are insufficient; those provisions were reviewed but are not reproduced as citations here. Both quoted § 3395 passages come from the same regulatory section (subdivisions (e) and (e)(6)) and are not independent of one another; the § 3396 quotation is drawn from the separate, independent regulation, § 3396(e)(2)(A). This is a description of a general regulatory requirement, not a determination of whether any particular workplace of the employer's has reached these thresholds or has implemented these measures.

ACCLIMATIZATION AND TRAINING REQUIREMENTS
Both standards define 'Acclimatization' the same way and require close observation of employees during an acclimatization period. 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3395(b) defines it as temporary adaptation of the body to work in the heat, and states: 'Acclimatization peaks in most people within four to fourteen days of regular work for at least two hours per day in the heat.' Consistent with that timeframe, § 3395(g)(2) requires that 'An employee who has been newly assigned to a high heat area shall be closely observed by a supervisor or designee for the first 14 days of the employee's employment,' and § 3395(g)(1) separately requires close observation of all employees during a defined 'heat wave.' The indoor standard imposes a parallel 14-day observation requirement in § 3396(g)(2): 'An employee who has been newly assigned to any of the following shall be closely observed by a supervisor or designee for the first 14 days of employment,' tied to the same temperature and work-condition triggers described in a companion clause of this information sheet.

Both standards also require employee and supervisor training before work that should reasonably be anticipated to expose the employee to the risk of heat illness. 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3395(h)(1) requires that 'Effective training in the following topics shall be provided to each supervisory and non-supervisory employee before the employee begins work that should reasonably be anticipated to result in exposure to the risk of heat illness,' covering environmental and personal risk factors, the employer's water/shade/cool-down/first-aid procedures, the importance of frequent water consumption, and, per § 3395(h)(1)(D), 'The concept, importance, and methods of acclimatization pursuant to the employer's procedures.' Both standards require separate supervisor training on those same topics plus supervisor-specific procedures, and § 3396 further requires training on the additional control measures the indoor standard adds.

  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3395 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 3395, subd. (b) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/3395.html)
  "An employee who has been newly assigned to a high heat area shall be closely observed by a supervisor or designee for the first 14 days of the employee's employment."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3395 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 3395, subd. (g)(2) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/3395.html)
  "An employee who has been newly assigned to any of the following shall be closely observed by a supervisor or designee for the first 14 days of employment:"
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3396 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 3396, subd. (g)(2) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/3396.html)
  "Effective training in the following topics shall be provided to each supervisory and non-supervisory employee before the employee begins work that should reasonably be anticipated to result in exposure to the risk of heat illness:"
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3395 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 3395, subd. (h)(1) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/3395.html)
  "The concept, importance, and methods of acclimatization pursuant to the employer's procedures under subsection (i)(4)."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3395 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 3395, subd. (h)(1)(D) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/3395.html)
  Known gap: This clause draws on two formally independent regulations, § 3395 (outdoor) and § 3396 (indoor); the 14-day observation quotations from each section are drawn from a single subdivision within that section, (g)(2), and are not independent of the other quotations from the same section used elsewhere in this clause. This clause does not independently quote every training topic listed in § 3395(h)(1)(A) through (I) or § 3396(h)(1)(A) through (I) — only the risk-factor, acclimatization, and general training-trigger language is quoted; the remaining listed topics (signs and symptoms of heat illness, reporting procedures, emergency-response and emergency-medical-services procedures) are described only in summary based on the fetched text. This clause also does not independently quote the supervisor-training subdivisions, § 3395(h)(2) and § 3396(h)(2), beyond stating that they exist and require training on the same and supervisor-specific topics. This is a description of a general regulatory requirement, not a determination of whether any particular employee or supervisor of the employer's has received this training or has been observed as the regulations describe.

THE WRITTEN HEAT ILLNESS PREVENTION PLAN REQUIREMENT
Both standards require a written plan, and both allow that plan to be folded into an employer's existing Injury and Illness Prevention Program. For outdoor workplaces, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3395(i) states: 'The employer shall establish, implement, and maintain, an effective heat illness prevention plan,' and separately requires: 'The plan shall be in writing in both English and the language understood by the majority of the employees and shall be made available at the worksite to employees and to representatives of the Division upon request.' The same subdivision states that this Heat Illness Prevention Plan 'may be included as part of the employer's Illness and Injury Prevention Program required by section 3203,' and must at minimum contain procedures for water and shade, the high-heat procedures, emergency response procedures, and acclimatization methods.

For indoor workplaces, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3396(i) imposes the same core written-plan duty: 'The employer shall establish, implement, and maintain an effective Heat Illness Prevention Plan.' It likewise permits that plan to be included as part of the employer's IIPP under § 3203 or its outdoor Heat Illness Prevention Plan under § 3395, and requires the plan to contain, at minimum, procedures for water, cool-down areas, the temperature/heat-index measurement and control measures described in a companion clause of this information sheet, emergency response procedures, and acclimatization procedures.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "The employer shall establish, implement, and maintain, an effective heat illness prevention plan."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3395 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 3395, subd. (i) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/3395.html)
  "The plan shall be in writing in both English and the language understood by the majority of the employees and shall be made available at the worksite to employees and to representatives of the Division upon request."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3395 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 3395, subd. (i) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/3395.html)
  "The employer shall establish, implement, and maintain an effective Heat Illness Prevention Plan."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3396 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 3396, subd. (i) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/3396.html)
  Known gap: This clause quotes both § 3395(i) and § 3396(i) because they are formally independent regulations, each imposing its own written-plan duty, even though a single written document may in practice satisfy both where an employer's operations are subject to both standards; the two § 3395(i) quotations in this clause are both drawn from that same subdivision of that same regulation and are not independent of one another. This clause does not independently quote every item on either standard's minimum-content list beyond the general summary given here (procedures for water/shade or water/cool-down, the temperature-triggered procedures, emergency response, and acclimatization); readers should not assume this clause states the full text of either list. This is a description of a general regulatory requirement, not a representation that the employer has or has not adopted a written Heat Illness Prevention Plan, and this information sheet is not itself that plan.

The outdoor standard ties the shade requirement to a specific temperature threshold. 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3395(d)(1) states: 'Shade shall be present when the temperature exceeds 80 degrees Fahrenheit.' Once that threshold is crossed, the employer must maintain one or more shaded areas at all times employees are present, and the amount of shade present 'shall be at least enough to accommodate the number of employees on recovery or rest periods, so that they can sit in a normal posture fully in the shade without having to be in physical contact with each other,' per the same subdivision. Below 80 degrees Fahrenheit, § 3395(d)(2) requires the employer either to provide shade on the same terms or to provide timely access to shade upon an employee's request. Employees must be allowed and encouraged to take a preventative cool-down rest in the shade whenever they feel the need to do so, per § 3395(d)(3).

The indoor standard uses the term 'cool-down area' rather than shade, and adds a temperature ceiling for that area. 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3396(d)(1) requires the employer to have and maintain one or more cool-down areas at all times employees are present, sized on the same normal-posture, no-physical-contact standard as the outdoor shade requirement, and states that 'the temperature in indoor cool-down areas shall be maintained at less than 82 degrees Fahrenheit, unless the employer demonstrates it is infeasible.'

expectedJSON.body:
Both standards impose additional obligations once the temperature crosses a second, higher threshold, beyond the water and shade/cool-down requirements described elsewhere in this information sheet. Under the outdoor standard, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3395(e) provides: 'The employer shall implement high-heat procedures when the temperature equals or exceeds 95 degrees Fahrenheit,' and those procedures — required only of the specific industries listed in § 3395(a)(2) — include maintaining effective communication with employees, observing employees for signs of heat illness, designating employees authorized to call for emergency medical services, reminding employees to drink water, and holding pre-shift meetings. For employees in agriculture specifically, § 3395(e)(6) requires that 'the employer shall ensure that the employee takes a minimum ten minute net preventative cool-down rest period every two hours' once temperatures reach 95 degrees or above.

The indoor standard instead requires the employer to measure temperature and heat index and apply control measures once a work area meets one of the § 3396(a)(2) conditions described in a companion clause of this information sheet. 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3396(e)(2)(A) requires that 'Engineering controls shall be used to reduce and maintain both the temperature and heat index to below 87 degrees Fahrenheit when employees are present, or to reduce the temperature to below 82 degrees Fahrenheit where employees wear clothing that restricts heat removal or work in high radiant heat areas, except to the extent that the employer demonstrates such controls are infeasible.' Where feasible engineering controls are not sufficient to reach those thresholds, the same subdivision requires the use of administrative controls and, where still insufficient, personal heat-protective equipment.

expectedJSON.body:
Both standards define 'Acclimatization' the same way and require close observation of employees during an acclimatization period. 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3395(b) defines it as temporary adaptation of the body to work in the heat, and states: 'Acclimatization peaks in most people within four to fourteen days of regular work for at least two hours per day in the heat.' Consistent with that timeframe, § 3395(g)(2) requires that 'An employee who has been newly assigned to a high heat area shall be closely observed by a supervisor or designee for the first 14 days of the employee's employment,' and § 3395(g)(1) separately requires close observation of all employees during a defined 'heat wave.' The indoor standard imposes a parallel 14-day observation requirement in § 3396(g)(2): 'An employee who has been newly assigned to any of the following shall be closely observed by a supervisor or designee for the first 14 days of employment,' tied to the same temperature and work-condition triggers described in a companion clause of this information sheet.

Both standards also require employee and supervisor training before work that should reasonably be anticipated to expose the employee to the risk of heat illness. 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3395(h)(1) requires that 'Effective training in the following topics shall be provided to each supervisory and non-supervisory employee before the employee begins work that should reasonably be anticipated to result in exposure to the risk of heat illness,' covering environmental and personal risk factors, the employer's water/shade/cool-down/first-aid procedures, the importance of frequent water consumption, and, per § 3395(h)(1)(D), 'The concept, importance, and methods of acclimatization pursuant to the employer's procedures.' Both standards require separate supervisor training on those same topics plus supervisor-specific procedures, and § 3396 further requires training on the additional control measures the indoor standard adds.

Both standards require a written plan, and both allow that plan to be folded into an employer's existing Injury and Illness Prevention Program. For outdoor workplaces, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3395(i) states: 'The employer shall establish, implement, and maintain, an effective heat illness prevention plan,' and separately requires: 'The plan shall be in writing in both English and the language understood by the majority of the employees and shall be made available at the worksite to employees and to representatives of the Division upon request.' The same subdivision states that this Heat Illness Prevention Plan 'may be included as part of the employer's Illness and Injury Prevention Program required by section 3203,' and must at minimum contain procedures for water and shade, the high-heat procedures, emergency response procedures, and acclimatization methods.

For indoor workplaces, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3396(i) imposes the same core written-plan duty: 'The employer shall establish, implement, and maintain an effective Heat Illness Prevention Plan.' It likewise permits that plan to be included as part of the employer's IIPP under § 3203 or its outdoor Heat Illness Prevention Plan under § 3395, and requires the plan to contain, at minimum, procedures for water, cool-down areas, the temperature/heat-index measurement and control measures described in a companion clause of this information sheet, emergency response procedures, and acclimatization procedures.
